day_by_day.morning: Arrival — Flight TP lands at 13:00, so no morning activities. Take the Aerobus or Metro (Linha Vermelha) from Aeroporto de Lisboa to central Lisbon (~30–40 min, €2–4). Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Baixa-Chiado neighbourhood on foot — a perfect, free introduction to Lisbon. Stroll along Rua Augusta, cross the famous Praça do Comércio by the Tagus riverfront, and ride the historic Elevador de Santa Justa (€5.30 round trip or free with a Lisboa Card) for panoramic views. Get your bearings and soak in the city atmosphere.
day_by_day.evening: Wander into the Alfama district as the sun sets. Catch a free viewpoint (miradouro) at Portas do Sol or Miradouro de Santa Luzia for golden-hour views over the Tagus. Listen for live Fado music drifting from local tascas — some smaller venues have free or low-cost Fado nights.

meals.breakfast: Eat on the plane or grab a quick pastel de nata (custard tart, ~€1.20) and a coffee (€0.80) at a local padaria near the hotel upon arrival.
meals.lunch: Pick up a fresh sandwich or bifana (pork roll, ~€2–3) from a local snack bar in Baixa — look for spots away from the main tourist squares for better prices.
meals.dinner: Tasca do Chico or a similar neighbourhood tasca in Alfama — look for the prato do dia (daily special) which typically includes soup, main course, bread, and a drink for €8–12. Try caldo verde soup and grilled sardines or bacalhau.

day_by_day.notes: Day 1 is intentionally light given the afternoon arrival. Buy a rechargeable Viva Viagem card (€0.50) at the airport Metro station and load it with credit for cheap public transport throughout your stay (single trips ~€1.61). Keep receipts — some restaurants offer a small discount if you ask for the fiscal receipt (fatura).

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Belém Tower (Torre de Belém) and the Jerónimos Monastery — two UNESCO World Heritage Sites from Portugal's Age of Discovery. The monastery is a masterpiece of Manueline architecture and costs €10 (free on Sunday mornings until 14:00 — consider swapping this to Sunday to save money). Belém Tower entry is €6. Combo tickets available for ~€12. Arrive early (opens 10:00) to beat crowds.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue exploring Belém on foot — visit the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos, €6 entry or admire free from outside) and stroll along the riverside promenade. Head to the nearby Museu de Arte Popular (free or low-cost) or simply enjoy the gardens. Take Tram 15E or Bus 728 back toward the city centre (~€1.61 with Viva Viagem card).
day_by_day.evening: Explore the lively Bairro Alto neighbourhood. Browse independent shops and street art, then settle in for the evening as the area comes alive. If budget allows, catch a short Fado performance at a community cultural centre (some offer shows for €5–10, far cheaper than tourist Fado houses).

meals.breakfast: Start the day like a local — coffee and pastel de nata at the legendary Pastéis de Belém bakery (the original since 1837, ~€1.40 per tart). Budget ~€3–4 total.
meals.lunch: Grab a prego (steak sandwich) or a bifana from a snack bar near Belém for €3–5, or pack a picnic from a local Pingo Doce supermarket (Belém area) with local cheeses, bread, and fruit for under €5.
meals.dinner: Head to Mercado de Campo de Ourique — a local food market less touristy than Time Out Market, with authentic stalls offering petiscos (Portuguese tapas) and mains for €6–10. Try alheira sausage or piri-piri chicken.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6 km west of central Lisbon — take Tram 15E from Praça da Figueira (cheap and scenic). If you plan to visit on Sunday, swap Day 2 and Day 3 to get free entry to Jerónimos Monastery before 14:00. Wear comfortable shoes — Belém involves a lot of walking on cobblestones.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Museum of Ancient Art (Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga) — Portugal's most important art collection, featuring works by Hieronymus Bosch and Nuno Gonçalves. Entry is €6 (free on Sunday mornings until 14:00). Spend 2–3 hours exploring the collection and the beautiful garden terrace overlooking the Tagus.
day_by_day.afternoon: Stroll through the Chiado neighbourhood — Lisbon's cultural and literary heart. Visit the free Largo do Carmo square and the ruins of the Carmo Convent (€5 entry, fascinating roofless Gothic church destroyed in the 1755 earthquake). Browse the independent bookshops on Rua do Carmo and Rua Garrett. Pop into the beautiful Livraria Bertrand, the world's oldest operating bookshop (free to browse).
day_by_day.evening: Join the Time Out Market Food Tour experience — spend a few hours at Lisbon's iconic food hall sampling the best of Portuguese cuisine, from bacalhau to pastéis. Budget €15–25 for tastings (individual dishes range from €3–8, so you can control spending). The market is buzzing on Sunday evenings and is a fantastic way to try multiple local specialties in one place.

meals.breakfast: Café A Brasileira in Chiado (historic café, iconic Fernando Pessoa statue outside) — coffee and toast for ~€3–4. Slightly touristy but worth the experience once.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at a local café near the museum — soup and bread (~€3) or a simple tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese sandwich, €2–3) to save appetite for the evening market.
meals.dinner: Time Out Market — graze on petiscos and small plates. Try pastéis de bacalhau (salt cod cakes), pica-pau (marinated beef bites), and finish with a ginjinha (cherry liqueur, €1.50) from a street kiosk nearby.

day_by_day.notes: Sunday in Lisbon is quieter and great for museum visits. Many museums offer free entry Sunday mornings — plan accordingly. The Chiado area is hilly; the free Elevador da Bica or Elevador da Glória funiculars (€3.80 one way, or included in transport passes) can save your legs. Keep an eye out for the free Sunday Feira da Ladra flea market in Campo de Santa Clara in Alfama — a great spot for vintage finds and local atmosphere.

day_by_day.morning: Deep dive into Alfama, Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighbourhood. Climb to the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) — entry is €15 but the surrounding free streets and viewpoints are equally rewarding. Alternatively, skip the paid entry and explore the free Miradouro da Graça and Miradouro do Monte (the highest viewpoint in Lisbon) for stunning panoramas. Wander through the labyrinthine medieval alleyways of Alfama.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the free Igreja de São Vicente de Fora church exterior and the nearby Panteão Nacional (National Pantheon, €4 entry) — a stunning baroque dome with a rooftop terrace and views over the Tagus. Then head to the Feira da Ladra flea market (Tuesdays and Saturdays — if this doesn't fall on those days, substitute with a walk along the LX Factory area in Alcântara). End the afternoon with a walk along the Tagus waterfront promenade (Ribeira das Naus — free).
day_by_day.afternoon_note: If Day 4 falls on a Tuesday, the Feira da Ladra flea market runs all day — perfect for budget souvenir hunting.
day_by_day.evening: Take the historic Tram 28E — Lisbon's most famous tram route — from Martim Moniz through Alfama, Graça, Estrela, and back (~€3 with Viva Viagem card). It's a sightseeing experience in itself. Finish the evening in the Intendente neighbourhood, an up-and-coming local area with affordable bars and authentic tascas.

meals.breakfast: Padaria (local bakery) near the hotel — croissant or pão com manteiga (bread with butter) and a galão (milky coffee) for €2–3.
meals.lunch: Tasca in Alfama — look for a hand-written menu on a chalkboard (a reliable sign of authentic, affordable food). Order the prato do dia for €8–10 including soup, main, and a glass of house wine.
meals.dinner: Cervejaria Ramiro (splurge option, ~€25–35pp) OR budget alternative: a simple marisqueira (seafood restaurant) in Intendente offering grilled fish, salad, and house wine for €12–15. Try amêijoas à Bulhão Pato (clams in garlic and white wine).

day_by_day.notes: Tram 28E gets extremely crowded — beware of pickpockets and consider riding it early morning or later evening to avoid peak tourist rush. The walk up to São Jorge Castle is steep — wear good shoes. Monday opening hours may vary for some smaller museums; always check in advance.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Parque das Nações (Park of Nations) — Lisbon's modern riverside district built for Expo 98. Stroll along the free riverside promenade, admire the Oriente railway station (a stunning free architectural landmark by Santiago Calatrava), and visit the Oceanarium (Oceanário de Lisboa, €21 — optional splurge, one of Europe's best aquariums, worth it for history and marine biology enthusiasts). The area is easily reached by Metro (Linha Vermelha, Oriente station).
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to central Lisbon for last-minute exploration. Browse the Rossio and Praça da Figueira squares — the historic heart of Pombaline Lisbon rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake. Visit the free exterior of the beautiful Estação do Rossio (Rossio train station) with its Moorish-style horseshoe arches. Pick up budget souvenirs: local olive oil, tinned fish (conservas), or ginjinha from local shops rather than tourist traps (Conserveira de Lisboa on Rua dos Bacalhoeiros is excellent and affordable).
day_by_day.evening: Final evening in Lisbon — head to Miradouro da Graça or Miradouro do Monte for a sunset drink. Buy a bottle of vinho verde (green wine, €3–5 from a supermarket) and enjoy it at the viewpoint with locals. End with a farewell dinner in Mouraria, Lisbon's multicultural neighbourhood adjacent to Alfama, where you'll find excellent and very affordable Portuguese and international food.

meals.breakfast: Café Nicola on Praça do Rossio — a historic café with affordable breakfast options. Coffee and pastel de nata for €3–4.
meals.lunch: Tasca or snack bar near Parque das Nações — the area has some affordable lunch spots away from the waterfront tourist restaurants. Alternatively, grab a francesinha (if you can find it in Lisbon — more Porto-style) or a simple prego for €4–6.
meals.dinner: Mouraria neighbourhood tasca — look for a menu offering cozido à portuguesa (Portuguese stew with meats and vegetables, a hearty classic) or grilled fish with potatoes and salad for €9–13. Toast to Lisbon with a final glass of Alentejo red wine.

day_by_day.notes: If your departure flight is on May 20th or later, use this evening to pack and prepare. Parque das Nações is best visited on a clear day for the riverside views — if weather is poor, substitute with the Museu do Azulejo (National Tile Museum, €5) for a beautiful and very budget-friendly deep dive into Portuguese azulejo tile history, highly recommended for history lovers. Keep €10–15 aside for Metro/bus to the airport on departure day.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear immigration, collect luggage, and take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) to reach Lisbon City Stay. Check in, freshen up, and get oriented with a map of the neighborhood.
day_by_day.afternoon: Take a leisurely self-guided stroll through the Chiado and Baixa districts near the hotel. Visit Praça do Comércio (Commerce Square) along the Tagus riverfront, walk up to Rua Augusta Arch, and browse the lively pedestrian streets. Stop at a local pastelaria to try your first pastel de nata and a bica (espresso).
day_by_day.evening: Ease into Lisbon with dinner in the Bairro Alto or Chiado area. Explore the atmospheric streets as the city comes alive at night. Visit a miradouro (viewpoint) such as Miradouro de Santa Catarina for a sunset view over the Tagus River.

meals.breakfast: Grab a snack at the airport or on arrival — try a café near the hotel for a light Portuguese sandwich (tosta mista) and coffee.
meals.lunch: Café A Brasileira or similar traditional café in Chiado — classic Portuguese soup (caldo verde) and a prego sandwich, around €10–14.
meals.dinner: Taberna da Rua das Flores (Chiado area) — a beloved traditional tasca offering seasonal Portuguese small plates and natural wines. Budget €25–35 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Day 1 is intentionally relaxed to account for travel fatigue. Keep the afternoon light and save energy for the full days ahead. Validate a Viva Viagem transport card at the Metro on arrival — it will be useful all week.

day_by_day.morning: Alfama District Walking Tour & Fado Show (morning portion): Join a guided walking tour of Alfama, Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood. Wind through narrow cobblestone streets, discover hidden miradouros, visit the São Jorge Castle exterior, and learn about the Moorish and medieval history of the city from a knowledgeable local guide.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue exploring Alfama independently after the tour. Visit the Feira da Ladra flea market (open Tuesdays and Saturdays — check if applicable) or explore the Se Cathedral (Lisbon Cathedral), one of the oldest churches in the city. Rest at a riverside café along the Alfama waterfront.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Alfama for the Fado Show portion of the experience. Enjoy an authentic Fado performance at a traditional casa de fado — Portugal's soulful, UNESCO-recognized musical tradition. Sip Portuguese wine and soak in the melancholic, beautiful atmosphere.

meals.breakfast: At the hotel or a nearby café — toasted bread with butter and jam, fresh orange juice, and a galão (milky espresso). €4–7.
meals.lunch: Tasca do Chico or a local tasca in Alfama — try grilled sardines or bacalhau à brás (codfish with eggs and potatoes). €12–18 per person.
meals.dinner: Dinner is typically included or paired with the Fado show venue. Expect traditional Portuguese cuisine — grilled fish, cured meats, cheese, and local wine. Budget €35–45 per person including the show.

day_by_day.notes: Book the Alfama Walking Tour & Fado Show in advance, especially for weekends. Wear comfortable shoes — Alfama's cobblestones are steep and uneven. The Fado shows typically begin around 20:00–21:00.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Tower & Jerónimos Monastery Visit: Take Tram 15E or a rideshare to the Belém district (about 20 minutes from central Lisbon). Begin with the Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking UNESCO World Heritage Site and masterpiece of Manueline architecture, built to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. Explore the ornate cloisters and church interior.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk five minutes to the Belém Tower (Torre de Belém), the iconic 16th-century fortress on the Tagus River and another UNESCO monument from Portugal's Age of Discovery. Afterward, visit the nearby Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) and enjoy a riverside walk. Stop at the famous Pastéis de Belém bakery — the original home of the pastel de nata since 1837.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon. Explore the Príncipe Real neighborhood, known for its elegant 19th-century mansions, independent boutiques, and relaxed garden square. Enjoy a calm evening dinner in this charming, slightly upscale residential district.

meals.breakfast: Hotel breakfast or a café near the hotel before departing for Belém. €5–8.
meals.lunch: Pastéis de Belém for iconic custard tarts (€1.20 each), then a proper lunch at Solar dos Presuntos or a riverside café in Belém — grilled fish or a bifanas (pork sandwich). €14–20.
meals.dinner: Café de São Bento or Tasca da Esquina in the Príncipe Real / Campo de Ourique area — contemporary Portuguese cuisine with local ingredients. €25–35 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Book Jerónimos Monastery tickets online in advance to avoid queues — it is one of Lisbon's most visited sites. Belém is about 6 km west of the city center; Tram 15E from Praça da Figueira is the most scenic route.

day_by_day.morning: National Museum of Ancient Art & Chiado Exploration: Visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (MNAA), Portugal's most important art museum, housing masterpieces including Hieronymus Bosch's 'The Temptation of St. Anthony' and a remarkable collection of Portuguese paintings, decorative arts, and artifacts spanning centuries of history. Allow 2–2.5 hours.
day_by_day.afternoon: Time Out Market Food Tour: Head to the iconic Time Out Market in Cais do Sodré for a curated Portuguese food experience. Sample your way through the best stalls — from petiscos (Portuguese tapas) and fresh seafood to artisan cheeses, charcuterie, ginjinha (cherry liqueur), and traditional desserts. This is one of the best ways to taste a wide variety of Portuguese cuisine in one place.
day_by_day.evening: Stroll along the revitalized LX Factory, a creative hub in a former 19th-century industrial complex (especially lively on Tuesdays and weekends). Browse local design shops, street art, and enjoy a drink at one of the hip bars before heading to dinner.

meals.breakfast: Café near the hotel or Mercado de Campo de Ourique (a local neighborhood food market) — fresh pastries, fruit, and coffee. €5–8.
meals.lunch: Time Out Market is your lunch — budget €15–25 for a satisfying spread of multiple tastings across several stalls.
meals.dinner: O Corvo or Zé da Mouraria in the Mouraria/Intendente area — honest, affordable Portuguese home cooking. €18–28 per person.

day_by_day.notes: The Time Out Market can get crowded after 13:00; arriving around noon is ideal. The MNAA is closed on Mondays, so Tuesday is perfect. LX Factory has a large Sunday market if you prefer to visit on weekends instead.

day_by_day.morning: Mouraria Neighborhood Food & History Walk: Join a local guide for a deep-dive into Mouraria, Lisbon's historic Moorish quarter and the birthplace of Fado. Discover the neighborhood's layered history — from the Moorish occupation to its working-class 20th-century identity — while tasting traditional foods at local vendors, bakeries, and family-run shops along the way.
day_by_day.afternoon: Free afternoon for personal exploration. Options include: visiting the Museu do Azulejo (National Tile Museum) to learn about Portugal's iconic azulejo tile tradition, browsing independent shops in Intendente square, or simply wandering and soaking up the city at your own pace. Pick up souvenirs — look for quality tinned fish, local wine, or handmade ceramics.
day_by_day.evening: Final dinner in Lisbon — celebrate the trip with a special meal. Return to the Baixa-Chiado area for a memorable last evening. Enjoy a walk along the illuminated Rua Augusta and a final ginjinha at A Ginjinha bar near Rossio Square, a beloved Lisbon institution since 1840.

meals.breakfast: Hotel breakfast or a final visit to a local pastelaria — enjoy your last galão and pastel de nata. €4–7.
meals.lunch: Included tastings during the Mouraria Food & History Walk — supplemented by snacks from local vendors. Budget €10–15 extra if desired.
meals.dinner: Cervejaria Ramiro (for seafood lovers) or Taberna Albricoque — a slightly elevated but still mid-range Portuguese dining experience for a memorable final meal. €30–45 per person.

day_by_day.notes: Book the Mouraria Food & History Walk in advance as group sizes are typically small. If departing early the next day, pack bags the night before and confirm any airport transfer or transport. Cervejaria Ramiro does not take reservations — arrive before 19:30 to avoid a long wait.

meals.lunch: Late lunch at Cantinho do Avillez (Chef José Avillez's beloved bistro in Chiado) — try the cod fritters and slow-cooked duck rice.
meals.dinner: Dinner included as part of the Fado Show experience in Alfama, featuring traditional Portuguese cuisine paired with local wines.

Explore the stunning 16th-century Belém Tower and the breathtaking Jerónimos Monastery, both UNESCO World Heritage Sites and masterpieces of Manueline architecture. Learn about Portugal's golden Age of Discovery with an expert guide.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and enjoy a relaxed evening in the upscale Príncipe Real neighborhood. Visit a curated wine bar for a premium Portuguese wine tasting — explore Douro reds, Alentejo whites, and aged Madeira wines with a sommelier.

meals.breakfast: Lavish breakfast at the hotel's restaurant — fresh fruit, smoked salmon, local cheeses, and freshly baked breads.
meals.lunch: After the Belém visits, dine at Feitoria Restaurant (1 Michelin star, inside the Altis Belém Hotel) overlooking the Tagus River — exceptional contemporary Portuguese cuisine.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Alma (Chef Henrique Sá Pessoa, 2 Michelin stars) in Chiado — a masterclass in refined Portuguese gastronomy with a tasting menu and wine pairing.

day_by_day.notes: Book Feitoria and Alma well in advance as both are highly sought-after. The Jerónimos Monastery can be crowded on weekends — arriving early in the afternoon helps. Don't miss the original Pastéis de Belém bakery for the world-famous custard tarts.

day_by_day.morning: National Museum of Ancient Art & Chiado Exploration — Begin with a private guided visit to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (MNAA), Portugal's most important art museum. Marvel at masterworks including Nuno Gonçalves' polyptych panels, Flemish paintings, and priceless decorative arts spanning centuries of Portuguese and global heritage.
day_by_day.afternoon: Mouraria Neighborhood Food & History Walk — Venture into Mouraria, Lisbon's historic Moorish quarter and the birthplace of Fado. Walk with a local expert guide through its vibrant streets, tasting traditional street foods, visiting hidden local eateries, and uncovering stories of the city's multicultural history. Discover spice markets, tiled facades, and the soul of old Lisbon.
day_by_day.evening: Sunset drinks at a premium rooftop bar — Sky Bar at Bairro Alto Hotel offers panoramic views over Lisbon's rooftops and the Tagus River. Follow with a private dinner experience featuring a curated menu.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel, followed by a stop at a Chiado café for a mid-morning coffee and almond croissant.
meals.lunch: Light tapas-style lunch during the Mouraria Food Walk — petiscos including chouriço, presunto, local olives, and fresh bread with olive oil at a family-run tasca.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Belcanto (Chef José Avillez, 2 Michelin stars) — Lisbon's most celebrated fine dining restaurant with a creative tasting menu inspired by Portuguese culinary tradition.

day_by_day.notes: Sunday mornings can be quieter at the MNAA — ideal for a more intimate museum experience. Belcanto reservations should be made weeks or months in advance. The Mouraria walk is best enjoyed at a slow, exploratory pace.

day_by_day.morning: Day trip to Sintra — Hire a private driver for a full morning excursion to the enchanting UNESCO-listed town of Sintra, just 40 minutes from Lisbon. Visit the fairy-tale Pena Palace with its vivid colors and Romantic architecture perched above the clouds, and explore the mysterious Quinta da Regaleira with its initiatic well and esoteric gardens.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue exploring Sintra with a visit to the Moorish Castle ruins for sweeping panoramic views over the Atlantic coastline and surrounding forests. Alternatively, drive to the dramatic Cabo da Roca — the westernmost point of continental Europe — for a spectacular coastal experience before returning to Lisbon.
day_by_day.evening: Back in Lisbon, unwind with a private Portuguese wine and cheese tasting experience arranged at the hotel or a premium enoteca in Príncipe Real. Enjoy a curated selection of aged queijo da Serra, presunto ibérico, and rare regional wines.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at the hotel before departure to Sintra.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Incomum by Luis Santos in Sintra — a refined restaurant set in a historic villa, offering contemporary takes on traditional Sintra and Portuguese cuisine.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Loco (Chef Alexandre Silva, 1 Michelin star) back in Lisbon — an avant-garde tasting menu that pushes boundaries while honoring Portuguese ingredients and tradition.

day_by_day.notes: A private driver for the Sintra day trip is highly recommended over public transport for comfort and flexibility. Pena Palace can be busy — pre-book timed entry tickets online. Bring a light jacket as Sintra's hilltops can be cool and misty even in May.

day_by_day.morning: Leisurely final morning in Lisbon — Take a private guided walk through the elegant Avenida da Liberdade, Lisbon's grand Champs-Élysées-style boulevard. Browse luxury Portuguese boutiques and artisan shops for last-minute gifts: premium cork goods, hand-painted azulejo tiles, aged ginjinha liqueur, and fine Vinho Verde selections.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Fundação Calouste Gulbenkian — one of Europe's finest private art museums, set within beautiful gardens. Explore its world-class permanent collection spanning Egyptian antiquities, Islamic art, Impressionist paintings, and René Lalique jewelry. A peaceful and culturally rich finale to your Lisbon experience.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a restaurant of your choice from the trip's highlights, or try Taberna da Rua das Flores — a beloved Lisbon institution serving traditional petiscos in an intimate, candlelit setting. Toast to an unforgettable journey with a glass of aged Port wine.

meals.breakfast: Extended farewell breakfast at the hotel — savor every last bite of Portuguese pastries, local honey, and fresh-pressed orange juice.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at the Gulbenkian Museum café, set in the garden — fresh salads, seasonal soups, and Portuguese snacks in a tranquil setting.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Taberna da Rua das Flores or a return visit to a favorite restaurant from the week — paired with a bottle of vintage Douro wine and a final glass of 20-year Tawny Port.

day_by_day.notes: Check hotel checkout time and arrange luggage storage if your departure flight is in the evening. The Gulbenkian is closed on Tuesdays — if so, substitute with a visit to the MAAT (Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology) along the Tagus riverfront as an excellent alternative. Confirm return transfer to the airport well in advance.
